claim: Skeletal muscle stem cells (satellite cells) are essential for muscle regeneration.
source: Skeletal muscle stem cells (also known as satellite cells [SCs]) are essential for muscle regeneration and the regenerative activities of SCs are intrinsically governed by gene regulatory mechanisms, but the post-transcriptional regulation in SCs remains largely unknown.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that establishes the importance of satellite cells in muscle regeneration, drawing on established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Post-transcriptional regulation in satellite cells remains largely unknown.
source: Skeletal muscle stem cells (also known as satellite cells [SCs]) are essential for muscle regeneration and the regenerative activities of SCs are intrinsically governed by gene regulatory mechanisms, but the post-transcriptional regulation in SCs remains largely unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field regarding post-transcriptional regulation mechanisms in satellite cells.

claim: N(6)-methyladenosine (m6A) modification of RNAs is the most pervasive and highly conserved RNA modification in eukaryotic cells.
source: N(6)-methyladenosine (m6A) modification of RNAs is the most pervasive and highly conserved RNA modification in eukaryotic cells; it exerts powerful impact on almost all aspects of mRNA processing that is mainly endowed by its binding with m6A reader proteins.
evidence: This statement draws on established scientific consensus about m6A modifications in eukaryotic cells.

claim: m6A modification exerts powerful impact on almost all aspects of mRNA processing.
source: N(6)-methyladenosine (m6A) modification of RNAs is the most pervasive and highly conserved RNA modification in eukaryotic cells; it exerts powerful impact on almost all aspects of mRNA processing that is mainly endowed by its binding with m6A reader proteins.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the broad functional impact of m6A modifications on mRNA processing.

claim: The impact of m6A on mRNA processing is mainly endowed by its binding with m6A reader proteins.
source: N(6)-methyladenosine (m6A) modification of RNAs is the most pervasive and highly conserved RNA modification in eukaryotic cells; it exerts powerful impact on almost all aspects of mRNA processing that is mainly endowed by its binding with m6A reader proteins.
evidence: This statement reflects established mechanistic understanding of how m6A modifications exert their effects through reader proteins.

claim: YTHDC1 is an essential regulator of SC activation and proliferation upon acute injury-induced muscle regeneration.
source: Our results demonstrate that YTHDC1 is an essential regulator of SC activation and proliferation upon acute injury-induced muscle regeneration.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from the YTHDC1 knockout experiments and muscle regeneration assays shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The induction of YTHDC1 is indispensable for SC activation and proliferation.
source: The induction of YTHDC1 is indispensable for SC activation and proliferation; thus, inducible YTHDC1 depletion almost abolishes SC regenerative capacity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing YTHDC1 expression dynamics (Figure 1) and the effects of its depletion on SC function (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: Inducible YTHDC1 depletion almost abolishes SC regenerative capacity.
source: The induction of YTHDC1 is indispensable for SC activation and proliferation; thus, inducible YTHDC1 depletion almost abolishes SC regenerative capacity.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from the inducible knockout experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: LACE-seq identifies m6A-mediated binding targets of YTHDC1 in both SCs and mouse C2C12 myoblasts.
source: Mechanistically, transcriptome-wide profiling using LACE-seq in both SCs and mouse C2C12 myoblasts identifies m6A-mediated binding targets of YTHDC1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the LACE-seq experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Splicing analysis defines splicing mRNA targets of m6A-YTHDC1.
source: Next, splicing analysis defines splicing mRNA targets of m6A-YTHDC1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the splicing analysis data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Nuclear export analysis leads to the identification of potential mRNA export targets of m6A-YTHDC1 in SCs and C2C12 myoblasts.
source: Furthermore, nuclear export analysis also leads to the identification of potential mRNA export targets of m6A-YTHDC1 in SCs and C2C12 myoblasts;interestingly, some mRNAs can be regulated at both splicing and export levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the subcellular fractionation and RNA-seq data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Some mRNAs can be regulated by m6A-YTHDC1 at both splicing and export levels.
source: Furthermore, nuclear export analysis also leads to the identification of potential mRNA export targets of m6A-YTHDC1 in SCs and C2C12 myoblasts;interestingly, some mRNAs can be regulated at both splicing and export levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the overlap analysis between splicing and export targets shown in Figure 6.

claim: YTHDC1 interacts with a myriad of factors governing mRNA splicing, nuclear export, and transcription in myoblasts.
source: Lastly, we map YTHDC1 interacting protein partners in myoblasts and unveil a myriad of factors governing mRNA splicing, nuclear export, and transcription, among which hnRNPG appears to be a bona fide interacting partner of YTHDC1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-IP/MS experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: hnRNPG appears to be a bona fide interacting partner of YTHDC1.
source: Lastly, we map YTHDC1 interacting protein partners in myoblasts and unveil a myriad of factors governing mRNA splicing, nuclear export, and transcription, among which hnRNPG appears to be a bona fide interacting partner of YTHDC1.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP/MS data and validation experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Quiescent satellite cells are uniquely labeled by the expression of paired box (Pax) transcription factor Pax7.
source: This is accomplished by satellite cells (SCs) that normally lie quiescent and uniquely labeled by the expression of paired box (Pax) transcription factor Pax7 (Fujita and Crist, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Fujita and Crist, 2018).

claim: Upon injury, the master myogenic regulator MyoD is expressed to enable rapid activation of SCs.
source: Upon injury, the master myogenic regulator MyoD is expressed to enable rapid activation of SCs, which then expand as proliferating myoblasts; the myoblasts then differentiate and fuse into myofibers to repair the damaged muscle, while a subset self-renews to restore the quiescent SC pool.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about satellite cell activation and the role of MyoD.

claim: Activated SCs expand as proliferating myoblasts.
source: Upon injury, the master myogenic regulator MyoD is expressed to enable rapid activation of SCs, which then expand as proliferating myoblasts; the myoblasts then differentiate and fuse into myofibers to repair the damaged muscle, while a subset self-renews to restore the quiescent SC pool.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about satellite cell lineage progression.

claim: Myoblasts differentiate and fuse into myofibers to repair damaged muscle.
source: Upon injury, the master myogenic regulator MyoD is expressed to enable rapid activation of SCs, which then expand as proliferating myoblasts; the myoblasts then differentiate and fuse into myofibers to repair the damaged muscle, while a subset self-renews to restore the quiescent SC pool.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about muscle regeneration processes.

claim: A subset of satellite cells self-renews to restore the quiescent SC pool.
source: Upon injury, the master myogenic regulator MyoD is expressed to enable rapid activation of SCs, which then expand as proliferating myoblasts; the myoblasts then differentiate and fuse into myofibers to repair the damaged muscle, while a subset self-renews to restore the quiescent SC pool.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about satellite cell self-renewal.

claim: Deregulated SC activity contributes to the development of many muscle diseases.
source: Deregulated SC activity contributes to the development of many muscle diseases; it is thus imperative to understand the way SCs contribute to regeneration.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the role of satellite cell dysfunction in muscle diseases.

claim: Both transcriptional and post-transcriptional gene regulations constitute key mechanisms governing SC activities.
source: Intrinsically, both transcriptional and post-transcriptional gene regulations constitute key mechanisms governing SC activities (Chen et al., 2021b; Relaix et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2021b; Relaix et al., 2021).

claim: m6A exerts powerful impact on almost all aspects of mRNA processing, including alternative splicing, nuclear export, stability maintenance, and translational efficiency.
source: m6A is the most pervasive and highly conserved RNA modification in eukaryotic cells and exerts powerful impact on almost all aspects of mRNA processing, including alternative splicing, nuclear export, stability maintenance, and translational efficiency, thus regulating diverse cellular processes (Shi et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Shi et al., 2019).

claim: RNA m6A modification is catalyzed by a multicomponent methyltransferase complex comprising METTL14, METTL3, WTAP, etc.
source: It is widely accepted (Murakami and Jaffrey, 2022; Shi et al., 2019) that RNA m6A modification is catalyzed by a multicomponent methyltransferase complex (the 'writer') comprising METTL14, METTL3, WTAP, etc., and can be removed by specific demethylases (the 'erasers'), including FTO and ALKBH5.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Murakami and Jaffrey, 2022; Shi et al., 2019).

claim: m6A can be removed by specific demethylases including FTO and ALKBH5.
source: It is widely accepted (Murakami and Jaffrey, 2022; Shi et al., 2019) that RNA m6A modification is catalyzed by a multicomponent methyltransferase complex (the 'writer') comprising METTL14, METTL3, WTAP, etc., and can be removed by specific demethylases (the 'erasers'), including FTO and ALKBH5.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Murakami and Jaffrey, 2022; Shi et al., 2019).

claim: Reader proteins that bind m6A are considered key effectors and executors of m6A functions.
source: However, it is the so-called 'reader' proteins that bind m6A and impart the epitranscriptomic information engraved in RNA m6A to functional signals; thus, these proteins are considered key effectors and executors of m6A functions.
evidence: This statement reflects established understanding of the role of m6A reader proteins in mediating m6A functions.

claim: YTH domain family proteins (YTHDF1, YTHDF2, YTHDF3, YTHDC1, and YTHDC2) specifically recognize m6A sites through YTH domain.
source: So far, a category of m6A readers has been identified and classified as several families, among which YTH domain family proteins, YTHDF1, YTHDF2, YTHDF3, YTHDC1, and YTHDC2, specifically recognize m6A sites through YTH domain and are the most well-known readers.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about YTH domain family proteins and their m6A recognition mechanism.

claim: YTHDC1 is a unique m6A reader because of its dominant location in the nucleus.
source: YTHDC1 is a unique m6A reader because of its dominant location in the nucleus endowing its post-transcriptional regulatory functions such as pre-mRNA splicing (Kasowitz et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2016), mRNA export (Lesbirel et al., 2018; Roundtree et al., 2017), and mRNA stabilization (Shima et al., 2017; Widagdo et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing YTHDC1's nuclear localization and functions.

claim: YTHDC1 has post-transcriptional regulatory functions including pre-mRNA splicing, mRNA export, and mRNA stabilization.
source: YTHDC1 is a unique m6A reader because of its dominant location in the nucleus endowing its post-transcriptional regulatory functions such as pre-mRNA splicing (Kasowitz et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2016), mRNA export (Lesbirel et al., 2018; Roundtree et al., 2017), and mRNA stabilization (Shima et al., 2017; Widagdo et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work demonstrating these functions.

claim: YTHDC1 promotes exon inclusion of targeted mRNAs in Hela cells by recruiting pre-mRNA splicing factor SRSF3 while blocking SRSF10 binding.
source: The pioneer study from (Xiao et al., 2016) shows that YTHDC1 promotes exon inclusion of targeted mRNAs in Hela cells by recruiting pre-mRNA splicing factor SRSF3 while blocking SRSF10 binding (Xiao et al., 2016); however, in a separate study (Roundtree et al., 2017), YTHDC1 interacting with SRSF3 facilitates the delivery of methylated mRNAs to export receptor NXF1 for cytoplasmic export, pointing to YTHDC1 and SRSF3 as adaptor proteins coupling mRNA splicing and export (Roundtree et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Xiao et al., 2016).

claim: YTHDC1 interacting with SRSF3 facilitates the delivery of methylated mRNAs to export receptor NXF1 for cytoplasmic export.
source: The pioneer study from (Xiao et al., 2016) shows that YTHDC1 promotes exon inclusion of targeted mRNAs in Hela cells by recruiting pre-mRNA splicing factor SRSF3 while blocking SRSF10 binding (Xiao et al., 2016); however, in a separate study (Roundtree et al., 2017), YTHDC1 interacting with SRSF3 facilitates the delivery of methylated mRNAs to export receptor NXF1 for cytoplasmic export, pointing to YTHDC1 and SRSF3 as adaptor proteins coupling mRNA splicing and export (Roundtree et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Roundtree et al., 2017).

claim: YTHDC1 and SRSF3 function as adaptor proteins coupling mRNA splicing and export.
source: The pioneer study from (Xiao et al., 2016) shows that YTHDC1 promotes exon inclusion of targeted mRNAs in Hela cells by recruiting pre-mRNA splicing factor SRSF3 while blocking SRSF10 binding (Xiao et al., 2016); however, in a separate study (Roundtree et al., 2017), YTHDC1 interacting with SRSF3 facilitates the delivery of methylated mRNAs to export receptor NXF1 for cytoplasmic export, pointing to YTHDC1 and SRSF3 as adaptor proteins coupling mRNA splicing and export (Roundtree et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Roundtree et al., 2017) and represents an inference from the described mechanism.

claim: Recent evidence implicates YTHDC1 in epigenetic and transcriptional control.
source: Interestingly, rapidly evolving evidence from the past two years implicates YTHDC1 in epigenetic and transcriptional control (Kan et al., 2022; Wei and He, 2021; Akhtar et al., 2021), (Lee et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to recent work.

claim: Many m6A regulators were dynamically expressed in the SC lineage progression course.
source: As a result, we found that many m6A regulators were dynamically expressed in the lineage progression course (Figure 1B–C and Figure 1—source data 1), reflecting their possible importance in controlling different phases of SC activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Ythdc1 mRNA was expressed at all stages of SC lineage progression with the highest level in FISCs.
source: Specifically, we found the reader Ythdc1 mRNA was expressed at all stages with the highest level in FISCs (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: YTHDC1 protein showed a very low level in FISC, an evident increase in activating cells (ASC-24 hr) and continued increase in proliferating cells (ASC-48 hr).
source: By western blotting (WB) and immunofluorescence (IF) (Figure 1E and F), we observed a very low level of YTHDC1 protein in FISC, an evident increase in activating cells (ASC-24 hr) and continued increase in proliferating cells (ASC-48 hr); YTHDF1 and YTHDF2 reader proteins appeared to show similar expression dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blotting and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: YTHDF1 and YTHDF2 reader proteins showed similar expression dynamics to YTHDC1.
source: By western blotting (WB) and immunofluorescence (IF) (Figure 1E and F), we observed a very low level of YTHDC1 protein in FISC, an evident increase in activating cells (ASC-24 hr) and continued increase in proliferating cells (ASC-48 hr); YTHDF1 and YTHDF2 reader proteins appeared to show similar expression dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blotting and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: YTHDC1 protein was predominantly detected in the nucleus but not cytoplasm.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Xiang et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2016), YTHDC1 protein was predominantly detected in the nucleus but not cytoplasm (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1F and citations to prior studies.

claim: YTHDC1 is predominantly located in the nuclear portion of C2C12 myoblasts.
source: This was also confirmed in mouse C2C12 cell line (a commonly used surrogate for ASCs) by fractionation assay (Figure 1G), suggesting its possible nuclear regulatory functions in myoblast cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by fractionation assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: YTHDC1's nuclear localization suggests its possible nuclear regulatory functions in myoblast cells.
source: This was also confirmed in mouse C2C12 cell line (a commonly used surrogate for ASCs) by fractionation assay (Figure 1G), suggesting its possible nuclear regulatory functions in myoblast cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed nuclear localization of YTHDC1.

claim: Freshly isolated SCs (FISCs) are considered as early activating cells due to the disruption of their niche by the isolation process.
source: Freshly isolated SCs (FISCs) by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) are considered as early activating cells due to the disruption of their niche by the isolation process (Machado et al., 2017); quiescent SCs (QSCs) were obtained through a pre-fixation step with paraformaldehyde (PFA) before the dissociation to preserve the quiescence status; FISCs were cultured for 24, 48, and 72 hr to obtain fully activated, proliferating, and differentiating SCs (ASC-24 hr, -48 hr, and -72 hr).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Machado et al., 2017).

claim: Massive immune cell infiltration was observed on the first day post injury in both control and iKO mice.
source: In both control (Ctrl) littermate and the iKO mice, massive immune cell infiltration was observed on the first day post injury (dpi) (data not shown); at 3 dpi, SCs were rapidly activated and reached a peak of proliferation in Ctrl (data not shown); by 5 dpi, they were mainly differentiating and labeled with eMyHC+ (expressed only in newly regenerating fibers) (Figure 2D and E), coinciding with the initiation of myofiber repair.
evidence: This claim is stated as an observation from the experiment, though the data is not shown.

claim: At 3 dpi, SCs were rapidly activated and reached a peak of proliferation in control mice.
source: In both control (Ctrl) littermate and the iKO mice, massive immune cell infiltration was observed on the first day post injury (dpi) (data not shown); at 3 dpi, SCs were rapidly activated and reached a peak of proliferation in Ctrl (data not shown); by 5 dpi, they were mainly differentiating and labeled with eMyHC+ (expressed only in newly regenerating fibers) (Figure 2D and E), coinciding with the initiation of myofiber repair.
evidence: This claim is stated as an observation from the experiment, though the data is not shown.

claim: By 5 dpi, SCs in control mice were mainly differentiating and labeled with eMyHC+.
source: In both control (Ctrl) littermate and the iKO mice, massive immune cell infiltration was observed on the first day post injury (dpi) (data not shown); at 3 dpi, SCs were rapidly activated and reached a peak of proliferation in Ctrl (data not shown); by 5 dpi, they were mainly differentiating and labeled with eMyHC+ (expressed only in newly regenerating fibers) (Figure 2D and E), coinciding with the initiation of myofiber repair.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: eMyHC is expressed only in newly regenerating fibers.
source: In both control (Ctrl) littermate and the iKO mice, massive immune cell infiltration was observed on the first day post injury (dpi) (data not shown); at 3 dpi, SCs were rapidly activated and reached a peak of proliferation in Ctrl (data not shown); by 5 dpi, they were mainly differentiating and labeled with eMyHC+ (expressed only in newly regenerating fibers) (Figure 2D and E), coinciding with the initiation of myofiber repair.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about eMyHC as a marker of newly regenerating muscle fibers.

claim: Muscle regeneration was nearly completely abolished in the iKO muscles.
source: As a striking contrast, muscle regeneration was nearly completely abolished in the iKO muscles; excessive immune infiltration was still present at 5 or 7 dpi with no signs of repair (Figure 2D); a sharp decrease of eMyHC+ myofibers was detected at both time points (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining and immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Excessive immune infiltration was still present at 5 or 7 dpi in iKO muscles with no signs of repair.
source: As a striking contrast, muscle regeneration was nearly completely abolished in the iKO muscles; excessive immune infiltration was still present at 5 or 7 dpi with no signs of repair (Figure 2D); a sharp decrease of eMyHC+ myofibers was detected at both time points (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A sharp decrease of eMyHC+ myofibers was detected at both 5 and 7 dpi in iKO muscles.
source: As a striking contrast, muscle regeneration was nearly completely abolished in the iKO muscles; excessive immune infiltration was still present at 5 or 7 dpi with no signs of repair (Figure 2D); a sharp decrease of eMyHC+ myofibers was detected at both time points (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A complete loss of Pax7+ cells was observed in iKO vs. Ctrl muscles after injury.
source: A complete loss of Pax7+ cells (Figure 2F and G) was also observed in iKO vs. Ctrl despite no difference was observed on uninjured muscles (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: No difference in Pax7+ cells was observed between iKO and Ctrl in uninjured muscles.
source: A complete loss of Pax7+ cells (Figure 2F and G) was also observed in iKO vs. Ctrl despite no difference was observed on uninjured muscles (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: At 14 dpi, injured Ctrl muscles were largely repaired.
source: At 14 dpi, injured Ctrl muscles were largely repaired (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Regeneration was never observed in iKO muscles even at 28 dpi.
source: But the regeneration was never observed even at 28 dpi; iKO muscle remained significantly smaller than Ctrl (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: iKO muscle remained significantly smaller than Ctrl at 28 dpi.
source: But the regeneration was never observed even at 28 dpi; iKO muscle remained significantly smaller than Ctrl (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by muscle size data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The iKO cells displayed evident growth arrest when cultured for 24 or 48 hr.
source: To this end, FISCs from Ctrl or iKO mice were cultured for 24 or 48 hr; and indeed the iKO cells displayed evident growth arrest (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell culture and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Activation (24 hr) and proliferation (48 hr) were drastically inhibited in the iKO compared to the Ctrl as shown by EdU staining.
source: This was confirmed by 4 hr EdU treatment and staining; activation (24 hr) and proliferation (48 hr) were drastically inhibited in the iKO compared to the Ctrl (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU staining and quantification data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SCs on isolated single myofibers failed to proliferate in iKO as confirmed by EdU staining of fibers cultured for 48 hr.
source: On isolated single myofibers, SCs also failed to proliferate, confirmed by EdU staining of the fibers cultured for 48 hr (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU staining and quantification data on single myofibers shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A lower percentage of Pax7+ MyoD+ double positive cells were detected at both ASC-24 hr and 48 hr in the iKO compared to the Ctrl.
source: Consistently, staining for Pax7 and MyoD showed that a lower percentage of double positive cells were detected at both ASC-24 hr and 48 hr in the iKO compared to the Ctrl (Figure 3C); the protein levels of Pax7 and MyoD were also largely diminished in the iKO cells at 48 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining and quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The protein levels of Pax7 and MyoD were largely diminished in the iKO cells at 48 hr.
source: Consistently, staining for Pax7 and MyoD showed that a lower percentage of double positive cells were detected at both ASC-24 hr and 48 hr in the iKO compared to the Ctrl (Figure 3C); the protein levels of Pax7 and MyoD were also largely diminished in the iKO cells at 48 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The number of Pax7+ MyoD+ SCs was reduced at both 24 hr and 48 hr on single myofibers in iKO.
source: On single myofibers, the number of Pax7+ MyoD+ SCs was also reduced at both 24 hr and 48 hr (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining and quantification data on single myofibers shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A significant reduction of EdU+ cells was observed in the iKO compared to the Ctrl muscles in the in vivo EdU assay.
source: Lastly, in vivo EdU assay was performed (Figure 3E); EdU was injected 2 days after BaCl2 -induced injury and SCs were isolated 12 hr later for staining. A significant reduction of EdU+ cells was observed in the iKO compared to the Ctrl muscles (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo EdU assay data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: A total of 547 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified in iKO vs. Ctrl SCs with 431 down- and 116 upregulated in ASC-24 hr.
source: As a result, a total of 547 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified in iKO vs. Ctrl SCs with 431 down- and 116 upregulated in ASC-24 hr (Figure 3G and Supplementary file 1); and the downregulated genes were enriched for GO terms such as 'Nuclear division,' 'Chromosome segregation,' etc. (Figure 3G and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The downregulated genes in ASC-24 hr iKO were enriched for GO terms such as 'Nuclear division' and 'Chromosome segregation'.
source: As a result, a total of 547 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified in iKO vs. Ctrl SCs with 431 down- and 116 upregulated in ASC-24 hr (Figure 3G and Supplementary file 1); and the downregulated genes were enriched for GO terms such as 'Nuclear division,' 'Chromosome segregation,' etc. (Figure 3G and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A total of 1272 DEGs (556 down- and 716 upregulated) were identified in ASC-48 hr iKO vs. Ctrl.
source: Similarly, a total of 1272 DEGs (556 down- and 716 upregulated) were identified in ASC-48 hr (Figure 3H) and again the downregulated genes were enriched for similar GO terms as the above (Figure 3H and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The downregulated genes in ASC-48 hr iKO were enriched for similar GO terms as ASC-24 hr.
source: Similarly, a total of 1272 DEGs (556 down- and 716 upregulated) were identified in ASC-48 hr (Figure 3H) and again the downregulated genes were enriched for similar GO terms as the above (Figure 3H and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Decreased proliferation rate was observed in two independent AID-YTHDC1 clones treated with IAA for both 48 hr and 72 hr.
source: In line with the results obtained from ASCs, decreased proliferation rate was observed in two independent AID-YTHDC1 clones treated with IAA for both 48 hr and 72 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H and Figure 3I), strengthening that YTDHC1 functions to promote myoblast proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU assay data in C2C12 cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H and Figure 3I.

claim: Only the WT but not mutant YTHDC1 could partially rescue the proliferation defect caused by YTHDC1 degradation.
source: As expected, only the WT but not mutant YTHDC1 could partially rescue the proliferation defect caused by YTHDC1 degradation (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), suggesting that indeed YTHDC1 is essential to promote myoblast proliferation and this function is dependent on its m6A binding function.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: YTHDC1's function in promoting myoblast proliferation is dependent on its m6A binding function.
source: As expected, only the WT but not mutant YTHDC1 could partially rescue the proliferation defect caused by YTHDC1 degradation (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), suggesting that indeed YTHDC1 is essential to promote myoblast proliferation and this function is dependent on its m6A binding function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the rescue experiment results showing that m6A binding mutants cannot rescue the proliferation defect.

claim: A total of 2444 shared peaks corresponding to 951 genes were identified as YTHDC1 binding targets in ASC-48 hr.
source: As a result, a total of 2444 shared peaks corresponding to 951 genes were identified from comparing the four replicates and defined as YTHDC1 binding targets (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by LACE-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All LACE-seq replicates in ASCs were well correlated with each other (Pearson correlation coefficient: 0.82~0.91).
source: All of these replicates were well correlated with each other (Pearson correlation coefficient: 0.82~0.91).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of the LACE-seq replicates.

claim: YTHDC1 binding targets in ASCs were enriched for GO terms such as 'Cell projection organization' and 'Cell junction assembly'.
source: These genes were enriched for GO terms such as 'Cell projection organization,' 'Cell junction assembly,' etc. (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis of LACE-seq targets shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A total of 29107 shared peaks corresponding to 5897 genes were identified as YTHDC1 binding targets in C2C12.
source: A total of 29107 shared peaks corresponding to 5897 genes were identified as YTHDC1 binding targets (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by LACE-seq data analysis in C2C12 shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The two C2C12 LACE-seq replicates displayed high correlation (Pearson correlation coefficient: 0.96).
source: Our results showed that data from C2C12 was of very high quality with the two replicates displaying high correlation (Pearson correlation coefficient: 0.96).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of the C2C12 LACE-seq replicates.

claim: YTHDC1 binding targets in C2C12 were enriched for GO terms such as 'Cell projection organization' and 'Cell junction assembly'.
source: Very similar to the above result from ASCs, these genes were also enriched for a variety of GO terms such as 'Cell projection organization,' 'Cell junction assembly,' etc. (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis of LACE-seq targets shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 1501 out of the 2444 identified peaks in ASCs could be found in C2C12.
source: In fact, 1501 out of the 2444 identified peaks in ASCs could be found in C2C12 (Figure 4E and Supplementary file 2), testifying the success of the assay.

evidence: This claim is supported by EdU assay data after hnRNPG knockdown shown in Figure 7K.

claim: hnRNPG knockdown phenocopied YTHDC1 loss caused defect in cell proliferation.
source: To demonstrate the functional relevancy of hnRNPG in SCs, we knocked down hnRNPG in ASCs and found cell proliferation was reduced (Figure 7K), which phenocopied YTHDC1 loss caused defect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that both YTHDC1 and hnRNPG loss reduce proliferation.

claim: hnRNPG functions synergistically with YTHDC1 in promoting SC proliferation.
source: The finding thus demonstrates that hnRNPG functions synergistically with YTHDC1 in promoting SC proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that both proteins interact and have similar effects on proliferation.

claim: SRSF3 was identified as a binding partner of YTHDC1 in the co-IP/MS.
source: Furthermore, we also identified the well-known binding partners of YTHDC1, SRSF3 (Xiao et al., 2016) on the list (Figure 7E), strengthening its function in regulating splicing in myoblasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP/MS data shown in Figure 7E and is consistent with prior reports.

claim: All known THOC members (THOC7, 1, 6, 3, 5, and 2) were retrieved by YTHDC1 in the co-IP/MS.
source: Strikingly, all the known THOC members, including THOC7, 1, 6, 3, 5, and 2, were retrieved by YTHDC1 (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP/MS data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The interaction of YTHDC1 with THOC7 was validated in C2C12 by co-IP followed by WB.
source: We validated the interaction of YTHDC1 with THOC7 in C2C12 by co-IP followed by WB (Figure 7L), reinforcing YTHDC1 function in controlling mRNA export.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP/WB validation data shown in Figure 7L.

claim: The bulk of mRNA nuclear export is mediated by the TREX complex and the heterodimeric nuclear export receptor NXF1:NXT1.
source: The bulk of the mRNA nuclear export is a complex yet well-characterized process mediated by the TREX complex and the heterodimeric nuclear export receptor NXF1:NXT1 (Lesbirel et al., 2018; Lesbirel and Wilson, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Lesbirel et al., 2018; Lesbirel and Wilson, 2019).

claim: TREX has 14 known subunits with the multimeric THO complex as the core.
source: As the key initiating complex, TREX has 14 known subunits with the multimeric THO complex as the core.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the composition of the TREX complex.

claim: Some known transcriptional regulators including RTRAF, MED29, and MED11 were identified as YTHDC1 interacting partners.
source: Furthermore, we also identified some known transcriptional regulators, including RTRAF, MED29, and MED11 (Figure 7G), pointing to previously unknown means via which YTHDC1 may regulate transcription.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP/MS data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The identification of transcriptional regulators as YTHDC1 interacting partners points to previously unknown means via which YTHDC1 may regulate transcription.
source: Furthermore, we also identified some known transcriptional regulators, including RTRAF, MED29, and MED11 (Figure 7G), pointing to previously unknown means via which YTHDC1 may regulate transcription.
evidence: This is speculation about potential novel functions of YTHDC1 based on the identification of transcriptional regulators as interacting partners.

claim: This is the first study to identify potential functional m6A regulators in SCs and provides a holistic investigation of YTHDC1 function in SCs and muscle regeneration.
source: Until now the study of m6A regulation and function in SCs is scarce (Diao et al., 2021; Kudou et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2021). This is the first study to identify potential functional m6A regulators and provides a holistic investigation of a writer protein, YTHDC1 function in SCs and muscle regeneration.
evidence: This statement claims novelty by comparing to prior limited work in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The incompetence of SC activation/proliferation is the major cause of nearly blocked regeneration after acute injury-induced muscle damage in YTHDC1 iKO.
source: We believe the incompetence of SC activation/proliferation is the major cause of nearly blocked regeneration after acute injury-induced muscle damage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed defects in SC activation/proliferation and the blocked regeneration phenotype.

claim: YTHDC1 may play a critical role in QSC maintenance.
source: We also noticed decreased SC numbers after long-term loss of YTHDC1 (data not shown), suggesting that it may play a critical role in QSC maintenance.
evidence: This is speculation based on an observation of decreased SC numbers after long-term YTHDC1 loss, though the data is not shown.

claim: YTHDC1 plays an indispensable role in SCs and muscle regeneration, which is not replaceable by other m6A readers.
source: Our findings thus suggest that YTHDC1 plays an indispensable role in SCs and muscle regeneration, which is not replaceable by other m6A readers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the severe phenotype observed upon YTHDC1 loss.

claim: YTHDC1 selectively binds a subset but not all m6A-modified RNAs.
source: From out data, YTHDC1 selectively bound a subset but not all m6A-modified RNAs (Figure 4H and J).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that not all m6A-modified RNAs are bound by YTHDC1 in the LACE-seq and MeRIP-seq integration.

claim: YTHDC1 selectivity for m6A-modified RNAs could be achieved by dynamic multivalent interactions of YTHDC1, RNAs, and regulatory proteins that self-organize into distinct condensates within the nucleus.
source: This selectivity could be achieved by dynamic multivalent interactions of YTHDC1, RNAs, and regulatory proteins that self-organize into distinct condensates (nuclear subcompartments) within the nucleus (He and He, 2021; Widagdo et al., 2022), It is also worth pointing out that a large portion of the YTHDC1 binding targets do not seem to possess m6A modification (Figure 4H), suggesting that YTHDC1 may have m6A-independent functions.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of YTHDC1 selectivity, supported by citations to prior work on condensates.

claim: A large portion of YTHDC1 binding targets do not seem to possess m6A modification, suggesting that YTHDC1 may have m6A-independent functions.
source: This selectivity could be achieved by dynamic multivalent interactions of YTHDC1, RNAs, and regulatory proteins that self-organize into distinct condensates (nuclear subcompartments) within the nucleus (He and He, 2021; Widagdo et al., 2022), It is also worth pointing out that a large portion of the YTHDC1 binding targets do not seem to possess m6A modification (Figure 4H), suggesting that YTHDC1 may have m6A-independent functions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that not all YTHDC1 binding targets have m6A modification.

claim: It is commonly believed that YTHDC1 regulatory functions are largely dependent on its m6A binding capacity.
source: However, it is commonly believed that YTHDC1 regulatory functions are largely dependent on its m6A binding capacity (Chen et al., 2021a; Cheng et al., 2021; Sheng et al., 2021; Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement reflects established understanding in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: It is likely that m6A-modified RNAs may initiate the recruitment of YTHDC1 through the YTH m6A binding domain, then YTHDC1 promotes condensate formation through the two intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) independent of its m6A reading function.
source: Nevertheless, since YTHDC1 is now known to participate in liquid phase separation (Widagdo et al., 2022), it is likely that m6A-modified RNAs may initiate the recruitment of YTHDC1 through the YTH m6A binding domain, YTHDC1 then promotes condensate formation through the two intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) independent of its m6A reading function.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of YTHDC1 function in condensates, based on knowledge of its participation in liquid phase separation.

claim: About 12% of YTHDC1 binding peaks were mapped to retrotransposons in ASCs and 10% in C2C12 cells.
source: It is also interesting to notice that about 12% of YTHDC1 binding peaks were mapped to retrotransposons in ASCs and 10% in C2C12 cells (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: In mESCs, YTHDC1 silences retrotransposons to guard ES cell identity.
source: In mESCs, YTHDC1 silences retrotransposons to guard ES cell identity (Chen et al., 2021a; Liu et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021), it would thus be interesting to explore the possible functional relevancy of YTHDC1 regulation of retrotransposons in SCs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in mESCs.

claim: The observed proliferative defects upon YTHDC1 loss could be a combinatorial effect of many downstream targets that were enriched for a wide range of GO functions important for SC proliferation.
source: Of note, our study identifies a large number of splicing or/and export targets of m6A-YTHDC1, and they play a wide range of cellular functions directly or indirectly related to cellular proliferation. The observed proliferative defects upon YTHDC1 loss thus could be a combinatorial effect of many downstream targets that were enriched for a wide range of GO functions important for SC proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D and Figure 6G and L).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that YTHDC1 targets are enriched for diverse functions related to proliferation.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling is known to induce SC proliferation during adult skeletal muscle regeneration.
source: For example, canonical Wnt signaling is known to induce SC proliferation during adult skeletal muscle regeneration (Otto et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Otto et al., 2008).

claim: hnRNPG can co-transcriptionally interact with both RNAPII and m6A-modified nascent pre-mRNA to modulate RNAPII occupancy and alternative splicing.
source: Originally known as a hnRNP family splicing factor via interactions with SRSF3, SRSF7, SLM, SAFB1 (Elliott et al., 2019; Heinrich et al., 2009), it was later shown to bind with m6A-modified mRNAs, thus possessing m6A reader function. It can co-transcriptionally interact with both RNAPII and m6A-modified nascent pre-mRNA to modulate RNAPII occupancy and alterative splicing (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Zhou et al., 2019).

claim: hnRNPG's implicated role in transcription repression was reported.
source: Its implicated role in transcription repression was also reported (Elliott et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Elliott et al., 2019).

claim: Both hnRNPG and YTHDC1 are versatile m6A-dependent gene regulators.
source: Therefore, both hnRNPG and YTHDC1 are versatile m6A-dependent gene regulators yet no study so far has made functional connection between these two key m6A readers despite their physical interaction being mentioned (Heinrich et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about both proteins, supported by citations.

claim: No study so far has made functional connection between hnRNPG and YTHDC1 despite their physical interaction being mentioned.
source: Therefore, both hnRNPG and YTHDC1 are versatile m6A-dependent gene regulators yet no study so far has made functional connection between these two key m6A readers despite their physical interaction being mentioned (Heinrich et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field, supported by citations.

claim: It will be interesting to determine whether YTHDC1 deregulation is implicated in muscle-related diseases such as aging-associated sarcopenia.
source: It will also be interesting to determine whether YTHDC1 deregulation is implicated in muscle-related diseases such as aging-associated sarcopenia.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future research directions.

claim: YTHDC1 may modulate transcriptional events in myoblast nucleus.
source: Although this study mainly focuses on delineating its post-transcriptional actions, we believe that YTHDC1 also modulates transcriptional events in myoblast nucleus and hnRNPG seems to constitute an important co-factor that may synergistically regulate both splicing and transcription functions of YTHDC1.
evidence: This is speculation based on the identification of transcriptional regulators as YTHDC1 interacting partners.

claim: hnRNPG seems to constitute an important co-factor that may synergistically regulate both splicing and transcription functions of YTHDC1.
source: Although this study mainly focuses on delineating its post-transcriptional actions, we believe that YTHDC1 also modulates transcriptional events in myoblast nucleus and hnRNPG seems to constitute an important co-factor that may synergistically regulate both splicing and transcription functions of YTHDC1.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional relationship between YTHDC1 and hnRNPG.

claim: It will be interesting to explore whether YTHDC1, hnRNPG, and the target mRNAs self-organize into distinct condensates within the myoblast nucleus.
source: In addition, it will be interesting to explore whether YTHDC1, hnRNPG, and the target mRNAs self-organize into distinct condensates within the myoblast nucleus as emerging evidence suggests RNA, m6A readers, and co-factors can cooperatively form distinct nuclear condensates at specific genomic loci (Widagdo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms, supported by a citation to emerging evidence.

claim: YTHDC1 may transiently shuttle into the cytoplasm and execute unexpected post-transcriptional functions such as in mRNA destabilization.
source: Furthermore, although YTHDC1 is predominantly found in the nucleus of myoblast cells, it may transiently shuttle into the cytoplasm as described in Rafalska et al., 2004; Shima et al., 2017 and execute unexpected post-transcriptional functions such as in mRNA destabilization (Shima et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation about potential cytoplasmic functions of YTHDC1, supported by citations to prior work.
